title: Los Angeles conductors and their downbeats
summary: He rates conductors such as Billy May, Mancini, Rugolo and Newman.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: But L.A. is a funny place. I don't know what it is. I like to live there. But the music, I don't like it. I like a lot of the conductors in Los Angeles. I think my favorite conductor in Los Angeles is Jack Elliott. I've played for under (you say you "play under," you know, when you play for a conductor) Earl Fagin, a very, very fine conductor. But I don't think he conducts any more. I think he had a couple of heart attacks. He is a very fine musician. Billy May. You have to learn everybody's downbeat, you know; it's all different. Hank Mancini's downbeat is a long downbeat. Billy May comes right down on it. There's different guys like that. Pete Rugolo, you never know what he's going to do. Johnny Mandel can't conduct for shit, and he knows it. He can write like a mother, but he can't conduct. And Nelson Riddle is a bad conductor. He's a great writer, but he's a... You've got to learn how to follow him. You've got to learn how to follow Franz Waxman. And Dmitri...
Yeah. Or whoever. All those guys. Alfred Newman, easy to follow. All those different guys. I never worked for those guys in New York. I didn't come to New York to do that stuff. I came to New York to
play Jazz. So I didn't run into any of those famous whatever they got back there. And I didn't even want to meet 'em. I'd just play what I damn well please.
